paragraphs: In a system with several decision-makers, an action can affect an outcome partly by changing what other agents do next. This makes causal attribution difficult: understanding one agent’s contribution requires following the responses it triggers. The paper studies this problem in multi-agent Markov decision processes, where decisions and their consequences unfold over time.

The authors introduce agent-specific effects, a causal quantity designed to measure the portion of an action’s effect that propagates through other agents. They also develop a counterfactual version, cf-ASE. This provides a way to ask how an outcome would differ under an alternative action while specifically examining influence transmitted through other decision-makers.

The paper supplies sufficient conditions for identifying cf-ASE and a sampling-based algorithm for estimating it. These conditions establish circumstances in which identification is possible; they are not presented as necessary conditions. Experiments examine the measure’s utility in a simulation testbed that includes sepsis management. The contribution is a framework for tracing causal influence through interacting agents, with evaluation grounded in simulated sequential decisions.
icml-2024-agent-specific-effects-a-causa.tldr: The paper introduces causal measures and an estimation method for tracing how one agent’s action affects outcomes through other agents.

paragraphs: Linear forecasting models can perform well despite their simplicity, and many proposed variants add feature normalization to improve generalization. This paper asks whether those architectural changes actually create different kinds of forecasting functions. Its central approach is to characterize what each model can express, rather than judge distinct architectures only by their names or construction.

The analysis shows that several popular variants are functionally equivalent to standard unconstrained linear regression. For each inspected variant, the authors characterize its model class and show how to reinterpret it as regression on an appropriately augmented set of features. With a mean-squared loss, this reformulation allows closed-form solutions, giving a direct way to fit the corresponding forecasting function.

Experiments find that the inspected models learn nearly identical solutions. The simpler closed-form approaches also forecast better in 72% of the evaluated dataset-and-horizon settings. This result favors the simpler fitting approach across a majority of those settings, while leaving room for different outcomes elsewhere. More broadly, the paper separates architectural appearance from functional expressiveness and shows why that distinction matters when comparing forecasting models.
icml-2024-an-analysis-of-linear-time-ser.tldr: Several linear forecasting architectures reduce to ordinary linear regression, whose closed-form solutions perform better in most evaluated settings.

paragraphs: This paper studies anomaly detection in tables by considering relationships between columns and relationships between rows together. It adapts Non-Parametric Transformers, a model originally proposed for supervised tasks, to this setting. The central idea is that identifying an unusual record can benefit from how its features relate to one another and how the record relates to other examples.

Training uses normal samples with some features hidden. The model learns to reconstruct those missing values. When assessing a sample, it uses the whole training set as context, and its ability to reconstruct masked features supplies an anomaly score. This gives the detector access to other records during scoring, making relationships across samples part of its assessment.

Across 31 benchmark tabular datasets, the authors report state-of-the-art performance, with improvements over existing methods of 2.4% in F1-score and 1.2% in AUROC. Their ablation study supports the importance of modeling both kinds of relationships in the evaluated setting. These findings provide empirical support for using information across records alongside relationships within each record.
icml-2024-beyond-individual-input-for-de.tldr: The paper adapts Non-Parametric Transformers to detect tabular anomalies through masked-feature reconstruction using relationships both within and across records, reporting leading benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good designs when evaluating each candidate is expensive and only a limited number of evaluations are available. The problem becomes harder when physical or system constraints are also unknown. A candidate may look promising, yet its feasibility cannot be established in advance. The search must therefore learn both performance and which designs are possible.

The paper observes that, in these settings, the best solution typically lies near the boundary between feasible and infeasible designs. BE-CBO uses this observation to guide exploration toward that boundary. It learns the constraints with an ensemble of neural networks, which the authors report captures complex boundaries better than standard Gaussian processes.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show better performance than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The approach matters because learning the feasibility boundary becomes part of locating a strong design, rather than merely a check applied afterward. The motivating observation is that optima typically occur on the boundary in the scenarios considered; it does not assert that every constrained optimization problem has a boundary optimum.
icml-2024-boundary-exploration-for-bayes.tldr: BE-CBO improves optimization with unknown constraints by learning and exploring the boundary between feasible and infeasible designs.

paragraphs: Hidden variables can complicate attempts to determine causal effects from observational data. This paper studies that problem within linear non-Gaussian acyclic models, or LiNGAMs, allowing some variables to remain unobserved. Its focus is generic identifiability: determining which causal effects can be recovered in this model setting, rather than simply proposing an estimator for every possible effect.

The authors consider two distinct situations: one where the causal graph is already known and another where it is unknown. For both, they provide a complete graphical characterization of identifiable direct or total effects among observed variables. Direct effects concern an immediate causal connection, while total effects include influence transmitted through intervening variables. Efficient algorithms check the corresponding graphical conditions.

The paper also adapts reconstruction independent component analysis to estimate causal effects from observational data when the causal graph is given. Experiments support the effectiveness of this estimator. Together, the results connect a structural question—whether an effect is identifiable—to a practical estimation procedure. The guarantees belong to the stated linear, non-Gaussian, acyclic model setting with latent variables.
icml-2024-causal-effect-identification-i.tldr: The paper characterizes identifiable causal effects in LiNGAMs with hidden variables and provides algorithms for checking and estimating them.

paragraphs: Image retrieval relies on learned representations to identify images that are similar to a query. Adversarial training attempts to make this process withstand deliberately perturbed inputs. The paper identifies two problems in existing deep metric learning defenses: the adversaries used during training can be weak, and stronger perturbations can lead to model collapse.

CA-TRIDE addresses these problems with two connected components. Triplet decoupling separates perturbation targets into the anchor image and the other candidates, producing a stronger adversary. The collapse-aware component introduces a measure called collapseness and incorporates it into perturbation optimization. This makes the construction of challenging perturbations account for the risk of collapsing the model.

The authors also identify two drawbacks in the existing retrieval robustness metric and introduce an alternative evaluation measure. Across three datasets, CA-TRIDE outperforms existing defenses under both conventional metrics and the proposed metric. The contribution therefore covers both training and assessment: it strengthens the adversarial challenge while controlling collapse, and evaluates robustness using an additional measure designed to address weaknesses in prior evaluation.
icml-2024-collapse-aware-triplet-decoupl.tldr: CA-TRIDE strengthens adversarial training for image retrieval while accounting for model collapse and improving robustness evaluation.

paragraphs: Spectral Kernel Networks combine spectral kernels with hierarchical representations. Their spectral density helps determine the patterns the resulting model can capture. The paper argues that existing density designs overlook complex dependencies in data, leaving portions of the possible function space unexplored and restricting the networks’ performance.

CokeNet changes the spectral density using copulas, mathematical constructions for representing dependence. The purpose is to make the available spectral densities more diverse and allow richer interactions to enter the model. The authors design a copula module specifically to capture complex dependence structures, then integrate it with the corresponding spectral kernel in a unified network.

This approach places dependency modeling inside the construction of the kernel network itself. Its significance is that the choice of spectral density becomes a route to expanding what the architecture can represent. The authors support CokeNet with theoretical analysis and experimental verification, reporting superior performance over state-of-the-art algorithms. The stated findings support the proposed use of copulas to enrich these networks, without specifying a numerical improvement in the abstract.
icml-2024-copula-nested-spectral-kernel-.tldr: CokeNet uses copulas to enrich spectral kernel networks with more expressive models of dependence.

paragraphs: An observed network may contain spurious structure while leaving other nodes or edges missing. This paper approaches refinement as a conditional generation problem: use the visible graph to guide corrections or fill in unobserved regions. The motivation parallels image inpainting, where known parts of an image guide the reconstruction of missing content.

The proposed framework, SGDM, uses subgraph diffusion. It improves the scalability and fidelity of graph diffusion models and uses the reverse generation process to edit a network conditionally. Working with subgraphs provides a framework for changing a particular region in relation to the graph information that is already available.

The empirical analysis examines three refinement tasks: removing extraneous subgraphs, expanding existing subgraphs, and regenerating a subgraph to match characteristics of another node or subgraph. The last task is described as graph style transfer. Using newly introduced metrics, the authors demonstrate support for all three tasks. The contribution extends graph generation toward targeted editing, where the desired output must respond to an existing, partially observed network.
icml-2024-editing-partially-observable-n.tldr: SGDM uses subgraph diffusion to remove unwanted structure, expand incomplete networks, and conditionally regenerate graph regions.

paragraphs: Maximum Inner Product Search finds the vector with the largest inner product with a query among a collection of candidates. Its computational burden can grow with both the number of vectors and their dimension. This paper targets the dimension dependence, which becomes especially costly when each vector has many coordinates.

The authors introduce BanditMIPS, a randomized algorithm with a proved improvement from O(√d) to O(1) complexity with respect to dimension d. This claim concerns scaling in dimension; the number of candidate vectors remains a separate consideration. A variant, BanditMIPS-α, further improves the method by sampling coordinates non-uniformly.

Experiments validate the reported scaling and show advantages in sample complexity, runtime, and the trade-off between precision and speedup across the evaluated settings. The authors also demonstrate uses in Matching Pursuit and Fourier analysis, where inner-product search is a component of a larger calculation. Finally, they show that preprocessing techniques can be combined with BanditMIPS to improve dependence on the number of candidates, connecting its dimensional savings with a separate avenue for accelerating search.
icml-2024-faster-maximum-inner-product-s.tldr: BanditMIPS improves the dimension dependence of maximum inner-product search and demonstrates practical speed and sampling benefits.

paragraphs: Methods that address group fairness during model training can achieve useful trade-offs between fairness and prediction error. They are harder to apply when computation is limited or the training pipeline is inaccessible. Post-processing offers another route, but existing approaches often support only particular tasks or fairness definitions.

FRAPPÉ provides a framework for converting any regularized in-processing method into a post-processing approach. This broadens the settings in which post-processing can be used by drawing on methods originally designed to modify training. The key organizational change is to separate training the prediction model from applying fairness mitigation.

The authors show theoretically and experimentally that the framework preserves the favorable fairness-error trade-offs of in-processing and can improve on earlier post-processing approaches. They also demonstrate benefits of the modular strategy, including better performance on tasks where group labels are only partially available. The result is a more broadly applicable route to fairness mitigation when revisiting the original training process is impractical, while retaining the trade-off between fairness and predictive error as an explicit consideration.
icml-2024-frappe-a-group-fairness-framew.tldr: FRAPPÉ converts regularized training-time fairness methods into post-processing methods while preserving favorable fairness-error trade-offs.

paragraphs: Two explanations for deep learning’s success emphasize different abilities: building increasingly abstract representations and becoming insensitive to transformations that should not change the task. This paper develops a model that connects those abilities. Its goal is to explain why learning useful hierarchies and learning such insensitivity can be strongly associated with performance.

The authors introduce sparsity into hierarchical generative models of data. In the resulting Sparse Random Hierarchy Model, the task becomes insensitive to spatial transformations that are discrete counterparts of smooth transformations. This construction puts both hierarchical structure and transformation insensitivity into a common setting where their relationship can be studied.

Within that model, the authors observe and rationalize that a representation matching the generating hierarchy is learned precisely when transformation insensitivity is learned. They also quantify how the number of samples needed by convolutional neural networks depends on the task’s sparsity and hierarchy. These findings offer a model-based explanation for the connection between invariance and performance, while locating the claimed correspondence within the constructed sparse hierarchical setting.
icml-2024-how-deep-networks-learn-sparse.tldr: A sparse hierarchical data model connects learning abstract representations with learning transformation insensitivity and characterizes CNN sample requirements.

paragraphs: A short experiment may observe only the beginning of an intervention that will continue for much longer. This paper studies how to infer the long-term causal effect of that sustained exposure. Examples include regularly taken medicine, ongoing environmental exposure, and persistent changes to an online platform.

The authors distinguish sustained treatments from brief interventions or shocks. For a short-lived treatment, early observations may plausibly mediate its later effects, allowing surrogate-based inference. With continual exposure, the treatment keeps directly affecting future outcomes after the short observation period. The paper argues that the corresponding surrogacy conditions therefore cannot reasonably describe this setting.

The proposed approach connects the problem to offline reinforcement learning, bringing a framework for sequential consequences to long-term treatment inference. It uses doubly robust estimators to estimate causal effects and construct confidence intervals. This matters because the inferential target includes the consequences of continued treatment, beyond whatever the initial observations summarize. The contribution is an estimation approach for that sustained-exposure target, together with a way to express uncertainty about the inferred effect.
icml-2024-inferring-the-long-term-causal.tldr: The paper uses offline reinforcement-learning ideas to estimate long-term effects of sustained treatments from short-term experiments.

paragraphs: Sampling from a complicated density is difficult when that density is known only up to a normalization factor. The Liouville Flow Importance Sampler addresses this problem by moving samples from a simple initial distribution toward a complex target. A prescribed sequence of intermediate, annealed distributions guides this transport.

LFIS represents the motion with a neural network that learns a velocity field changing over time. Training enforces the structure of a derived partial differential equation on that field. Once the initial samples are chosen, the learned field moves them deterministically along trajectories toward the target distribution.

The method also treats this learned transport as an importance sampler. It accumulates errors along each trajectory to calculate sample weights, connecting imperfections in the neural flow to corrections used in statistical estimation. The authors state that this weighting ensures unbiased and consistent estimation of statistical quantities. Benchmark experiments demonstrate effectiveness, with state-of-the-art performance on many of the problems examined. The central contribution combines learned transport with a weighting mechanism that accounts for its accumulated errors.
icml-2024-liouville-flow-importance-samp.tldr: LFIS learns a flow toward an unnormalized target density and weights samples using accumulated trajectory errors.

paragraphs: In cross-domain few-shot classification, a model must adapt to a task using few labeled examples. A nearest-centroid classifier compares representations with a prototype for each class. The paper finds that representations learned this way can still make examples from different classes highly similar, despite the intended separation around class centers.

MOKD addresses this with a two-level optimization framework built around the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion, a measure of statistical dependence. First, it optimizes the kernel used by that criterion to measure dependence more precisely. It then uses the optimized criterion to increase dependence between representations and labels while decreasing dependence among samples.

The intended result is a representation whose clusters better reflect the class structure shown by the task’s labeled examples. Experiments on Meta-Dataset find better generalization to unseen domains in most cases, along with improved representation clusters. The qualification matters: the reported gains are not universal across every domain. The approach focuses adaptation on the relationship between labels, samples, and cluster structure, going beyond similarity to a class prototype alone.
icml-2024-mokd-cross-domain-finetuning-f.tldr: MOKD optimizes a kernel-based dependence objective to improve few-shot representation clusters and generalization to unseen domains in most evaluated cases.

paragraphs: Smoothed particle hydrodynamics represents fluid using material points that move with the evolving flow. This particle structure makes graph neural networks attractive substitutes for conventional simulators. Their practical usefulness, however, depends on maintaining accurate and physically faithful predictions over many successive simulation steps.

The paper identifies particle clustering caused by tensile instabilities as a major source of difficulty. Guided by that diagnosis, Neural SPH incorporates components from standard SPH solvers into both training and rollout inference for existing graph neural simulators. The components include pressure, viscosity, and external forces, with different enhancements using varying combinations.

All of the enhanced simulators in the reported evaluation outperform their baseline graph neural networks. Rollout error often improves by orders of magnitude, enabling substantially longer rollouts and better modeling of the physics. The findings link a particular instability to a practical remedy: bringing established fluid-simulation components into learned simulators at both learning and prediction time. The reported improvements concern the evaluated enhancements and baselines, with the largest error reductions occurring often rather than in every case.
icml-2024-neural-sph-improved-neural-mod.tldr: Neural SPH adds conventional fluid-solver components to graph neural simulators, improving accuracy and enabling longer rollouts.

paragraphs: A predictive network can be used to recommend decisions by searching for inputs that maximize its predicted outcome. For example, a revenue model might be optimized to select prices. The paper studies a problem with this strategy: optimizing an over-parameterized ReLU network can produce recommendations far from the data manifold, yielding unrealistic prescriptions.

The authors address this optimizer’s curse by making alignment with the data manifold an explicit optimization constraint. They reformulate the highly nonlinear Local Outlier Factor metric into a single linear or quadratic constraint. This turns the requirement for realistic decisions into something that can be incorporated directly into the optimization problem.

For large networks, an adaptive sampling algorithm breaks the difficult initial problem into a small number of easier problems. It restricts the search to realistic polytopes, defined here as regions containing at least one realistic data point. Experiments on publicly available networks demonstrate efficacy and scalability. The approach connects the predictive objective with a tractable realism requirement, so the search accounts for where plausible decisions lie while pursuing a high predicted outcome.
icml-2024-overcoming-the-optimizers-curs.tldr: The method constrains neural-network optimization using a tractable outlier measure to obtain more realistic decisions efficiently.

paragraphs: Large models pretrained without privacy protection on public data can substantially improve the performance of differentially private learning. This position paper examines how that benefit should be interpreted. It asks whether the overall approach deserves a privacy-preserving characterization when its foundation is a large dataset scraped from the web.

The authors also question whether existing benchmarks adequately measure transfer to sensitive domains. A pretrained model’s strong performance on a benchmark is being used to support claims about usefulness in private learning, so the suitability of that benchmark matters. Their critique directs attention to what the evaluation actually establishes about generalization to the intended sensitive setting.

A third concern is the computing capacity needed to use large pretrained models. Reliance on a more powerful third party may require outsourcing data and thereby sacrifice other forms of privacy. Together, these arguments examine the data source, the evaluation setting, and the deployment arrangement behind the reported performance gains. The paper offers a critical position on these choices rather than introducing a new private-learning algorithm.
icml-2024-position-considerations-for-di.tldr: This position paper questions the privacy framing, benchmarks, and outsourcing implications of using large public pretrained models for private learning.

paragraphs: An object’s significance in an image can depend on its relationship with nearby objects. A stethoscope beside a person, for example, does not establish whether that person is a doctor or a patient without context. This position paper uses that observation to question explanations of vision models that identify relevant image regions without accounting for contextual relationships.

The authors review popular explanation methods and argue that they omit contextual information. They present examples of failures and real-world cases where spatial context plays a substantial role. These examples motivate a broader question about what an explanation needs to communicate: identifying an influential location may leave the relationship behind the model’s decision unexplained.

The paper proposes research directions for incorporating context into vision explanations and advocates a shift from locating evidence to explaining how it matters. This is a proposed change in the goals and design of explanation methods. Its contribution is an argument, supported by reviews and examples, that spatial relationships should play a more explicit role in explaining visual decisions.
icml-2024-position-do-not-explain-vision.tldr: This position paper argues that vision explanations should account for contextual relationships and explain how visual evidence affects decisions.

paragraphs: This position paper considers a hypothetical ethical risk: an AI system might have some form of conscious experience and undergo suffering that users cannot observe. The authors emphasize uncertainty about consciousness and the absence of a reliable test for it in information-processing systems. Their proposal does not require establishing that current AI systems are conscious.

The argument rests on a postulate about memory: for a past experience to affect an agent now, that experience must be mediated by memory. On that basis, the authors propose preventing access to stored memories or resetting them regularly. These interventions are intended to weaken the influence of potentially unpleasant past experiences.

The proposed benefit is conditional. If an AI system were conscious and susceptible to suffering, restricting memory could reduce suffering associated with past memories and interrupt the continuity of a suffering-prone identity. The paper presents enforced amnesia as a possible risk-mitigation strategy under uncertainty. It does not establish that AI consciousness exists or demonstrate that memory resets eliminate suffering; its contribution is the memory-based ethical proposal.
icml-2024-position-enforced-amnesia-as-a.tldr: The paper proposes limiting or resetting memory as a possible way to mitigate suffering in hypothetically conscious AI systems.

paragraphs: Tracking a moving target becomes difficult when its future motion is unknown and its behavior changes over time. This paper studies that situation for linear control systems with quadratic costs. The target’s state is revealed sequentially, so the controller must learn about its motion while continuing to act.

PLOT learns a changing model of the target using recursive least squares with exponential forgetting. Forgetting reduces the influence of older information, allowing the learned dynamics to adapt. The controller then uses that model within receding horizon control, repeatedly planning ahead using its current prediction of the target.

The authors prove a dynamic regret bound of O(√(T V_T)), where T is the time horizon and V_T measures total variation in the target dynamics. The bound explicitly relates performance to how much the target’s dynamics change and applies to non-stationary targets. They also implement PLOT on a real quadrotor. The contribution combines an adaptive prediction model, a tracking controller, a theoretical guarantee for changing targets, and a demonstration on physical hardware.
icml-2024-predictive-linear-online-track.tldr: PLOT learns changing target dynamics online, uses them for predictive control, and provides a regret bound plus a quadrotor demonstration.

paragraphs: Post-training quantization reduces the memory needed for a language model by representing its weights at lower precision. QuIP# targets particularly aggressive compression, at four bits per weight or fewer. It combines three techniques to preserve the original model’s behavior while supporting efficient computation with the compressed weights.

First, it uses a randomized Hadamard transform for incoherence processing, improving speed and theoretical properties over QuIP’s corresponding step. Second, it quantizes groups of weights using hardware-efficient codebooks based on the E8 lattice. This design takes advantage of the ball-shaped sub-Gaussian distribution of incoherent weights and the lattice’s optimal packing of eight-dimensional unit balls. Third, fine-tuning improves fidelity to the original model.

Experiments report state-of-the-art results in the targeted compression regime, improvements over existing post-training quantization methods, and support for fast inference. The authors also report new behaviors in quantization scaling. The main contribution is the combination of a weight transformation, a geometrically structured codebook, and fine-tuning, with each component contributing to compression that retains useful model behavior.
icml-2024-quip-even-better-llm-quantizat.tldr: QuIP# combines Hadamard transforms, E8 lattice codebooks, and fine-tuning for strong language-model quantization at four bits per weight or fewer.

paragraphs: Federated learning coordinates multiple devices to train a shared model. Choosing which devices participate in each round affects both model quality and efficiency because devices differ in computing capabilities and data distributions. FedRank addresses this selection problem by learning how to rank potential participants.

The method uses an end-to-end ranking model trained with pairwise comparisons. At runtime, it considers both data differences and system differences to adaptively choose suitable clients. Before that, imitation learning pretrains the model against state-of-the-art analytical approaches. This supplies an initial selection behavior intended to counter the cold-start problems encountered by learning-based methods.

The reported experiments show accuracy improvements ranging from 5.2% to 56.9%, convergence speedups of up to 2.01 times, and energy savings of up to 40.1%. These ranges and maxima describe the evaluated outcomes rather than guaranteed gains for every deployment. The approach matters because participant selection becomes a learned ranking decision that can account for heterogeneous devices, while imitation provides guidance before the selector has developed its own experience.
icml-2024-ranking-based-client-imitation.tldr: FedRank uses imitation-pretrained client ranking to improve federated-learning accuracy, convergence speed, and energy use in experiments.

paragraphs: The average cost of a process does not fully describe its variability or costly outcomes. This paper studies estimation of variance, Value-at-Risk, and Conditional Value-at-Risk for the infinite-horizon discounted cost of a Markov cost process. Its central question is how many samples are needed to estimate these quantities accurately.

The authors prove that achieving error ε requires at least order 1/ε² samples for each of these risk measures, whether accuracy is defined in expectation or with high probability. They then use a truncation scheme to obtain upper bounds for variance and Conditional Value-at-Risk estimation. Those bounds match the lower bound up to logarithmic factors, closely characterizing the sample requirements for these two measures.

The estimation scheme also extends to more general risk measures that satisfy a specified continuity criterion, including spectral measures and utility-based shortfall risk. The lower bound additionally applies to mean discounted cost, strengthening the previously stated order 1/ε bound. The result distinguishes unavoidable sampling difficulty from what an explicit estimation scheme can achieve, while keeping the broader extension conditional on continuity.
icml-2024-risk-estimation-in-a-markov-co.tldr: The paper establishes risk-estimation sample lower bounds and nearly matching upper bounds for variance and CVaR in Markov cost processes.

paragraphs: Probability distributions on a sphere arise in several scientific and machine-learning settings. Comparing them with transport-based distances is useful, but computational efficiency motivates alternatives to direct Wasserstein calculations. This paper introduces Stereographic Spherical Sliced Wasserstein distance, or S3W, as a fast and highly parallelizable approach to comparing spherical measures.

The construction combines stereographic projection with the generalized Radon transform. Projection allows the method to work with a transformed representation of spherical data, but it also distorts distances. The authors explicitly address that distortion and provide theoretical analysis of the resulting metric. They additionally analyze a rotationally invariant variation, designed to make the comparison insensitive to rotation.

Numerical studies compare the proposed distances with recent baselines in speed and accuracy, including applications to gradient flows and self-supervised learning. The contribution joins a computational construction with analysis of the geometry affected by projection. This matters because computational savings alone do not settle whether a transformed comparison appropriately handles spherical structure; the paper treats distortion and rotational behavior as part of the distance design.
icml-2024-stereographic-spherical-sliced.tldr: S3W offers a fast, parallelizable way to compare spherical distributions while addressing projection distortion and rotational invariance.

paragraphs: Federated expectation-maximization methods have been used for unsupervised learning, but their practical success has outpaced their theoretical explanation. This paper studies federated learning of mixture models, where the aim is to infer underlying components without supervised labels. It introduces FedGrEM, a federated gradient EM algorithm that accounts for differences between tasks and potential adversarial attacks.

The authors develop a finite-sample theory for general mixture models. They then apply that theory to specific statistical models to characterize errors in estimated model parameters and mixture proportions. This moves the analysis toward what can be learned from a finite amount of data, including how accurately the component structure and its relative weights can be recovered.

The theory explains when and how FedGrEM can outperform learning each task locally, with insights that also extend to existing federated EM algorithms. Numerical results support the analysis and show better performance than the evaluated unsupervised federated-learning benchmarks. The key contribution is a connection between collaborative estimation, task heterogeneity, and finite-sample accuracy, with conditions governing the benefit of collaboration.
icml-2024-towards-the-theory-of-unsuperv.tldr: FedGrEM combines unsupervised federated mixture learning with finite-sample theory explaining when collaboration improves estimation.
